item.title: Postal codes and tessellations
item.description: From postal points to areas using Voronoi polygons
item.content:encoded:
From postal points to areas using Voronoi polygons

I recently published my project Postal codes of Spain, with estimated postal areas, an interactive map and GeoPackage downloads. But there is something we have not looked at yet: how do those address points become polygons? The answer is… Voronoi polygons.

What is a Voronoi polygon?

Imagine a few shops on a flat map. Which one is closest to your house? Ask that question for every location and give each shop its own color. The result is a Voronoi diagram, also known as a Voronoi tessellation, Voronoi decomposition, Voronoi partition or Dirichlet tessellation. This technique divides a plane into regions based on the distance to a given set of points.

In our example, each shop is a site, or generating point. Its Voronoi cell, also called a Thiessen polygon, contains the locations at least as close to that site as to any other. Along a shared edge, two sites are equally close. Where several cells meet, there may be a tie between more sites. With ordinary straight-line distance, the edges follow perpendicular bisectors between sites. Some cells extend indefinitely, so maps usually show them clipped to a study area.

The name honors Georgy Voronoi, who studied these partitions in the early twentieth century. The idea has earlier roots, including Dirichlet’s nineteenth-century work (hence the name Dirichlet tessellation). Pokojski and Pokojska (2018) review the history and geographical applications.

These partitions are useful for exploring proximity to shops or public services, assigning areas to weather stations and studying spatial patterns. For example, Thiessen polygons can supply area weights when estimating rainfall from rain gauges. The underlying question is always about the chosen distance: the nearest hospital in a straight line may not be the quickest one to reach.

A tiny example in R

Let’s start with five points in an imaginary square, including one at its center, using just sf and ggplot2. The coordinates have arbitrary units and no geographical coordinate reference system.

library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

# Define a common theme for the maps.
background <- "#faf8f2"
ink <- "#203b47"

theme_set(
  theme_void() +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = background, colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = background, colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = ink),
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", hjust = 0),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )
)

sites <- data.frame(
  site = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  x = c(2, 7, 3, 8, 5),
  y = c(2, 3, 8, 7, 5)
)

toy_points <- st_as_sf(sites, coords = c("x", "y"))

study_area <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(c(xmin = 0, ymin = 0, xmax = 10, ymax = 10)))

toy_cells <- toy_points |>
  st_union() |>
  st_voronoi(envelope = study_area) |>
  st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
  st_intersection(study_area)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = toy_cells,
    fill = c("#a8dadc", "#f4c89a", "#c6b8df", "#bfd59b", "#f2b5c4"),
    colour = "white", linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = toy_points, colour = "#203b47", size = 3) +
  geom_text(
    data = sites, aes(x, y, label = site),
    nudge_y = 0.5, colour = "#203b47", fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Five points, five Voronoi cells",
    subtitle = "Each location belongs to the closest site"
  )

Five points, five cells. The point E at (5, 5) has a bounded cell surrounded by the other four. The outer cells extend beyond the square and are clipped to its edges. st_union() collects the points into one geometry, st_voronoi() builds the diagram and st_intersection() clips it to our square. The colors help us tell the cells apart. We have not assigned any postal codes yet.

The diagram knows nothing about roads, rivers or administrative boundaries. As we move to postal points, we will need to make our choices about those boundaries explicit.

Before we start: what are we estimating?

The Spanish project uses CartoCiudad address points with their postal codes. It follows Goerlich (2022), who develops an idea presented by Sánchez (2020). The updated online version describes the method in detail.

For Slovenia, we will use GISCO’s postal points, retrieved with giscoR. There is an important difference here: a representative point for a code tells us much less than thousands of addresses with that code. Detailed addresses help the partition follow their distribution more closely, although proximity alone still cannot reproduce postal delivery decisions.

We have not established that Slovenian postal areas should follow municipal boundaries. Imposing those boundaries is a modeling choice for this exercise, inspired by the Spanish workflow, rather than a verified property of the Slovenian postal system.

This post explains the workflow. The polygons we create are not official postal boundaries, and this exercise does not validate the GISCO postal data.

Getting the data

First, let’s get the municipal boundaries and postal points. We use the 2024 release of both datasets.

library(giscoR)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)

municipalities <- gisco_get_lau(
  year = 2024, country = "SI", epsg = 3035
) |>
  select(GISCO_ID, LAU_NAME) |>
  st_make_valid()

raw_points <- gisco_get_postalcodes(
  year = 2024, country = "SI", epsg = 3035
)

We work in ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035), a projected coordinate system with coordinates in meters. This makes the 200 m and 50 m margins used later meaningful. Voronoi uses Euclidean distances in this plane, rather than road distances. The projection does not preserve every distance exactly either.

Before we start drawing, what have we actually downloaded?

postal_points <- raw_points |>
  mutate(POSTCODE = trimws(as.character(POSTCODE))) |>
  filter(!is.na(POSTCODE), POSTCODE != "") |>
  select(POSTCODE)

code_counts <- postal_points |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(POSTCODE, name = "points_per_code")

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Indicator = c(
    "Municipalities", "Downloaded points", "Points with a postal code",
    "Distinct postal codes", "Codes represented by one point"
  ),
  Value = c(
    nrow(municipalities), nrow(raw_points), nrow(postal_points),
    nrow(code_counts), sum(code_counts$points_per_code == 1)
  )
))
Indicator Value
Municipalities 212
Downloaded points 557
Points with a postal code 557
Distinct postal codes 557
Codes represented by one point 557

These counts give us a first look at the file, but they are not a quality check. They do not establish whether every code is present or whether the coordinates are correct. With one point per code, we will be drawing areas around representatives rather than estimating them from individual addresses.

Two points at exactly the same coordinates cannot generate separate Voronoi cells. We sort by postal code and keep the first point at each location, as in the original workflow. This is a reproducible tie-breaking rule, not evidence that the retained code is correct. The counts below show how many records we remove and how many locations have conflicting codes.

postal_points <- postal_points |> arrange(POSTCODE)

conflicts <- postal_points |>
  group_by(geometry) |>
  summarise(codes = n_distinct(POSTCODE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(codes > 1)

duplicates <- duplicated(postal_points$geometry)

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Indicator = c("Duplicate locations removed", "Locations with conflicting codes"),
  Value = c(sum(duplicates), nrow(conflicts))
))
Indicator Value
Duplicate locations removed 79
Locations with conflicting codes 16 

postal_points <- postal_points[!duplicates, ]

Starting with Ljubljana

Let’s pick Ljubljana and keep the points inside it. We use st_within() so that a point exactly on a shared boundary is not assigned to both neighboring municipalities.

city <- municipalities |> filter(LAU_NAME == "Ljubljana")

city_points <- st_filter(postal_points, city, .predicate = st_within)

base_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = city, fill = "#e8e4d8", colour = ink, linewidth = 0.4)

gisco_attr <- gisco_attributions()

base_map +
  geom_sf(data = city_points, colour = "#bd5137", size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Ljubljana: the starting point",
    subtitle = "A municipal boundary and points with postal codes",
    caption = gisco_attr
  )

Building the cells

Each cell contains locations at least as close to its generating point as to any other point. Cell boundaries occur where distances to two points are equal. For this first demonstration, we keep all interior points, without the margins used in the national workflow.

cells <- city_points |>
  st_union() |>
  st_voronoi(envelope = st_as_sfc(st_bbox(city))) |>
  st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
  st_sf(geometry = _)

base_map +
  geom_sf(data = cells, fill = NA, colour = "#bd5137", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = city_points, colour = ink, size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "An area of proximity for every point",
    subtitle = "Cells still extend beyond the municipal boundary",
    caption = "Own elaboration using data from Eurostat / GISCO, 2024"
  )

st_union() gathers the points so we build one diagram. One detail to keep in mind: envelope supplies a working extent, but does not clip the cells to the municipality. We need an intersection for that.

Clipping and recovering postal codes

It would be convenient if cells came out in the same order as the input points, but we should not rely on that. Instead, we recover each cell’s code with a spatial relationship before clipping. Each cell must contain exactly one generating point.

point_matches <- st_intersects(cells, city_points)

cells$POSTCODE <- city_points$POSTCODE[unlist(point_matches)]

clipped_geometry <- st_intersection(st_geometry(cells), st_geometry(city))

city_cells <- st_sf(
  POSTCODE = cells$POSTCODE[attr(clipped_geometry, "idx")[, 1]],
  geometry = clipped_geometry
)

city_areas <- city_cells |>
  group_by(POSTCODE) |>
  summarise(.groups = "drop") |>
  st_make_valid()

city_colours <- setNames(
  hcl.colors(nrow(city_areas), palette = "Dark 3"),
  sort(city_areas$POSTCODE)
)
city_labels <- st_sf(
  POSTCODE = city_areas$POSTCODE,
  geometry = st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(city_areas))
)

ggplot(city_areas) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = POSTCODE), colour = background, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_sf(
    data = city_points, shape = 21, fill = ink,
    colour = background, size = 2.4
  ) +
  geom_sf_text(
    data = city_labels,
    aes(label = POSTCODE), colour = ink, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = city_colours, guide = "none") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "From points to estimated areas",
    subtitle = "Cells clipped and merged by postal code",
    caption = "Teaching example · Not official postal boundaries"
  )

We intersect the geometry columns, then use the intersection’s idx matrix to recover each cell’s postal code. This keeps the attribute assignment explicit. Label positions are also calculated from geometries alone.

Grouping by postal code with summarise() merges the geometries. With many addresses sharing a code, their cells would dissolve into one geometry, possibly with several separate parts.

From one municipality to the whole country

Ljubljana is done. Now let’s repeat the operation for each component of each municipality. Municipalities can have separate pieces: normalizing to MULTIPOLYGON and then casting to POLYGON lets us handle them independently, without automatically extending a code to a piece with no points.

The municipality ID and name apply to every component, so we mark those attributes as spatially constant before splitting the geometries.

components <- municipalities |>
  st_set_agr("constant") |>
  st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  mutate(component_id = row_number())

Why use an inward margin?

In the Spanish project, we first select addresses within an inward margin of 200 m. If none are found, we try 50 m. This reduces the influence of points close to a boundary, where small mismatches between layers may affect their assignment.

There is no universal rule behind these numbers. Goerlich describes a 20 m margin. The 200 m and 50 m choices come from my implementation. We keep them here to explain that workflow, although sparse postal points make it easier to exclude useful information. Comparing other margins would be a useful next step.

select_points <- function(component, postal_points) {
  for (margin in c(200, 50)) {
    interior <- st_buffer(st_geometry(component), -margin)

    if (all(st_is_empty(interior))) next

    selected_points <- st_filter(postal_points, interior,
      .predicate = st_within
    )

    if (nrow(selected_points) > 0) {
      return(selected_points)
    }
  }

  postal_points[0, ]
}

The margin only selects points: the resulting areas cover the original component, not the smaller buffered geometry. If both attempts fail, we leave the component unassigned. We do not borrow the nearest point from outside the municipality.

Three cases, one function

There are three cases to handle. With no points, we keep the component and assign NA. If all selected points share a code, we assign it to the whole component. We only need Voronoi when several codes are present: no need to split an area that already has a single assignment.

build_areas <- function(component, postal_points) {
  selected_points <- select_points(component, postal_points)

  codes <- unique(selected_points$POSTCODE)

  if (length(codes) <= 1L) {
    component$POSTCODE <- if (length(codes)) codes else NA_character_
    return(component)
  }

  cells <- selected_points |>
    st_union() |>
    st_voronoi(envelope = st_as_sfc(st_bbox(component))) |>
    st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
    st_sf(geometry = _)

  point_matches <- st_intersects(cells, selected_points)

  cells$POSTCODE <- selected_points$POSTCODE[unlist(point_matches)]

  clipped_geometry <- st_intersection(
    st_geometry(cells),
    st_geometry(component)
  )

  result <- st_sf(
    POSTCODE = cells$POSTCODE[attr(clipped_geometry, "idx")[, 1]],
    geometry = clipped_geometry
  ) |>
    group_by(POSTCODE) |>
    summarise(.groups = "drop") |>
    st_make_valid()

  result$GISCO_ID <- component$GISCO_ID

  result$LAU_NAME <- component$LAU_NAME

  result$component_id <- component$component_id

  result
}

result <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(components)), function(i) {
  build_areas(components[i, ], postal_points)
}) |>
  bind_rows()

Handling unassigned areas

Can we fill any of the gaps? A component without points may belong to a municipality whose other components have information. We recover its code only if the municipality has one distinct recovered code. This is an imputation from the available data, not proof that the municipality really has just one code.

unique_codes <- result |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(POSTCODE)) |>
  distinct(GISCO_ID, POSTCODE) |>
  add_count(GISCO_ID) |>
  filter(n == 1)

unassigned_before <- sum(is.na(result$POSTCODE))

index <- match(result$GISCO_ID, unique_codes$GISCO_ID)

recoverable <- is.na(result$POSTCODE) & !is.na(index)

result$POSTCODE[recoverable] <- unique_codes$POSTCODE[index[recoverable]]

Before drawing the final map, let’s tidy up the geometries and keep only surfaces. Repairs can produce collections containing residual lines or points, which do not belong in an area layer. Dissolving by postal code also removes municipal boundaries between areas sharing that code.

keep_surfaces <- function(x) {
  geometry <- st_make_valid(st_geometry(x))

  geometry <- lapply(geometry, function(part) {
    if (!inherits(part, c("POLYGON", "MULTIPOLYGON", "GEOMETRYCOLLECTION"))) {
      return(st_multipolygon())
    }

    surfaces <- suppressWarnings(st_collection_extract(st_sfc(part), "POLYGON"))

    if (length(surfaces) == 0L || all(st_is_empty(surfaces))) {
      return(st_multipolygon())
    }

    st_cast(st_union(surfaces), "MULTIPOLYGON", warn = FALSE)[[1]]
  })

  st_geometry(x) <- st_sfc(geometry, crs = st_crs(x))

  x[!st_is_empty(x), ]
}

unassigned <- result |>
  filter(is.na(POSTCODE)) |>
  keep_surfaces()

postal_areas <- result |>
  filter(!is.na(POSTCODE)) |>
  group_by(POSTCODE) |>
  summarise(.groups = "drop") |>
  keep_surfaces() |>
  st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON")

The complete map

For the national overview, let’s color the areas by the first digit of their code. This keeps the map readable, without claiming that we have validated a classification of postal regions. Gray is reserved for unassigned components, with their own legend entry.

postal_colours <- c(
  "1" = "#007F7F", "2" = "#E87500", "3" = "#3B6FB6", "4" = "#A64E9A",
  "5" = "#649A32", "6" = "#D9AF00", "8" = "#B94350", "9" = "#6255A4",
  "Unassigned" = "#727A80"
)

postal_groups <- sort(unique(substr(postal_areas$POSTCODE, 1, 1)))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = municipalities, fill = "#d5d2ca", colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(
    data = postal_areas,
    aes(fill = substr(POSTCODE, 1, 1)), colour = background, linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = unassigned, aes(fill = "Unassigned"),
    colour = background, linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = postal_colours, name = "Postal code group",
    breaks = c(postal_groups, "Unassigned"),
    labels = c(paste0(postal_groups, "xxx"), "Unassigned")
  ) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(
    title = "Slovenia, point by point",
    subtitle = "Proximity areas clipped to municipal boundaries",
    caption = paste("Eurostat / GISCO, 2024 · Own elaboration",
      "Dark grey: unassigned areas · Estimated boundaries, not official",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  )

Checking the result

The map is ready, but let’s check the geometry before going further. Are the polygons valid? Do assigned and unassigned areas cover the territory? Are there any appreciable overlaps? We allow one square meter for numerical differences in the geometry operations.

territory <- st_union(st_geometry(municipalities))

coverage <- st_union(c(st_geometry(postal_areas), st_geometry(unassigned)))

difference_m2 <- as.numeric(sum(st_area(st_sym_difference(territory, coverage))))

overlap_m2 <- as.numeric(
  sum(st_area(postal_areas)) + sum(st_area(unassigned)) - sum(st_area(coverage))
)

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Indicator = c(
    "Codes with an estimated area", "Components assigned by municipal recovery",
    "Unassigned records", "Unassigned area (km²)",
    "Coverage difference (m²)", "Overlap (m²)"
  ),
  Value = round(c(
    nrow(postal_areas), sum(recoverable), nrow(unassigned),
    as.numeric(sum(st_area(unassigned))) / 1e6, difference_m2,
    overlap_m2
  ), 4)
))
Indicator Value
Codes with an estimated area 468.0000
Components assigned by municipal recovery 4.0000
Unassigned records 6.0000
Unassigned area (km²) 150.2033
Coverage difference (m²) 0.0000
Overlap (m²) -0.0002

These checks verify the geometry, not postal accuracy. We could cover an entire country with valid polygons and still have a poor approximation of its delivery areas.

Back to Spain

We now have the full sequence: points, proximity areas, clipping and merging by postal code. The same steps work with much more detailed addresses, such as the CartoCiudad data in my Spanish postal codes project.

The input data matters as much as the algorithm. With one representative point per code, Voronoi mainly maps distances between representatives. With address points, it can better approximate where each code’s addresses are concentrated. It still knows nothing about delivery routes, physical barriers or official boundaries.

We have not compared these results with an independent postal source for Slovenia. Before using them for analysis, we would need to review coverage, coordinates, the relationship with municipalities and sensitivity to the margins. For now, we have a working example that shows how the polygons are built, one step at a time.

The title is a nod to Muse’s album Black Holes and Revelations.

References

  • Goerlich, F. J. (2022). Elaboración de un mapa de códigos postales de España con recursos libres: Cómo evitar pagar por disponer de información de referencia (Working Paper No. 2022-3). Ivie. https://doi.org/10.12842/WPIVIE_0322 (Updated online version)
  • Hernangómez, D. (2026). Códigos postales de España (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23698418 (Project documentation)
  • Pokojski, W., & Pokojska, P. (2018). Voronoi diagrams – Inventor, method, applications. Polish Cartographical Review, 50(3), 141–150. https://doi.org/10.2478/pcr-2018-0009
  • Sánchez, J. I. (2020, November 13). Así hice el mapa de los códigos postales de España con SIG y datos abiertos. Nosolosig. Article

item.title: Postal codes of Spain
item.description: Estimated postal code areas from open data
item.content:encoded:
Estimated postal code areas from open data

Códigos postales de España provides estimated postal code areas for Spain, built from open address data from CartoCiudad and administrative boundaries. Explore the results on interactive maps and download the data for use in R, Python or QGIS.

Background

Postal code polygons are useful for linking addresses and statistics to areas on a map. According to Goerlich (2022), the Correos polygons available through CartoCiudad stopped being offered for download in early 2017. This project explores a reproducible alternative based on open address data.

An early reference is José Ignacio Sánchez’s 2020 article in NoSoloSIG, which describes how to estimate postal areas from CartoCiudad addresses using GIS tools. This project applies the approach developed in Francisco José Goerlich’s 2022 work, with its own choices for selecting addresses and handling areas without an assignment.

Maps and data

The project website includes interactive maps and two GeoPackage downloads: a full version for spatial analysis and a simplified version for visualization. Both include postal code areas and administrative areas pending assignment.

The data is shared under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license.

Interactive map

Search for a postal code or address, select a two-digit prefix and compare the estimated areas with CartoCiudad. The viewer uses the simplified data and does not display areas pending assignment. Its controls are in Spanish.

Open the map in a full window Viewer guide

Methodology

Following Goerlich’s approach, the workflow treats each separate component of an administrative area independently. When the selected addresses share a single postal code, it assigns that code to the whole component. When several codes are present, it builds Voronoi polygons around the address locations, clips them to the administrative boundary and merges areas with the same code. The final polygons are dissolved by postal code across provinces.

This implementation selects addresses using an inward buffer of 200 m, with a second attempt at 50 m if none are found, rather than the 20 m described by Goerlich. Components without selected addresses remain unassigned unless the municipality has a single postal code recovered from its other components. The administrative boundaries come from LAU2boundaries4Spain, by Francisco José Goerlich and Pedro Pérez Vázquez.

These are estimated areas, not official postal boundaries. Coverage depends on the source addresses and some areas remain unassigned. The repository documents the sources, methodology, limitations and steps to reproduce the data.

References

  • Centro Nacional de Información Geográfica. (n.d.). CartoCiudad [Data set]. https://www.cartociudad.es/web/portal/
  • Correos. (n.d.). Base de datos de códigos postales y capa cartográfica [Product information]. Product page
  • Goerlich, F. J. (2022). Elaboración de un mapa de códigos postales de España con recursos libres: Cómo evitar pagar por disponer de información de referencia (Working Paper No. 2022-3). Ivie. https://doi.org/10.12842/WPIVIE_0322 (Updated online version)
  • Goerlich, F. J., & Pérez Vázquez, P. (2025). Base de datos histórica de contornos municipales de España –LAU2boundaries4Spain– (Version 2) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15345101
  • Hernangómez, D. (2026). Códigos postales de España (Version 1.0.0) [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23698418 (Project documentation)
  • Instituto Geográfico Nacional. (n.d.). Servicios de visualización de CartoCiudad: Direcciones y códigos postales [WMS documentation]. Service documentation
  • Sánchez, J. I. (2020, November 13). Así hice el mapa de los códigos postales de España con SIG y datos abiertos. Nosolosig. Article

item.title: Large forest fires in Spain
item.description: EGIF reports, reconciled fire records and cartography with R
item.content:encoded:
EGIF reports, reconciled fire records and cartography with R

GIFs brings together structured data on large forest fires in Spain and R code for an infographic inspired by Dominic Royé’s firefly cartography. Here, GIF means gran incendio forestal: a fire with at least 500 hectares of forest area burned.

The project combines exports from MITECO’s General Forest Fire Statistics (EGIF) with its annual reports and provisional updates. It preserves source information and reconciliation notes so that users can trace how records were selected, grouped and located.

Two related data products

The collection currently provides two complementary views:

  • EGIF reports: 329 selected reports from 2010–2023. Each row has a unique egif_part_id and includes source fields, burned areas, cause, provenance, notes and coordinates where they can be interpreted.
  • Reconciled fires: 455 fire records from 2010–2026, used by the infographic. Each fire has a stable fire_id; a fire may bring together several EGIF reports.

These are different units of observation. Do not add the two tables’ row counts or burned areas together. The 500-hectare threshold is applied after explicitly documented groupings of reports belonging to the same fire.

EGIF takes priority when a documented match exists. Records without a match retain their original MITECO annual report or provisional update. Reports awaiting reconciliation keep an empty fire_id and are not automatically added as new fires, which helps avoid double counting.

Coverage and limitations

The fire-level records span February 27, 2010 to September 26, 2026. These are the first and last dates in the file, not evidence of complete annual coverage. The project is not a real-time monitoring service.

The documented reconciliation still has nine earlier fire records and eight selected EGIF reports awaiting a match. Two additional records retain their provisional source because their province has no reports in the 2023 EGIF export. That export contains no records for seven provinces, so an absence from these files should not be interpreted as an absence of fires.

The methodology explains source priority, explicit groupings and unresolved cases. The data guide documents the source exports and processing. The original ZIP files are preserved with SHA-256 checksums.

Coordinates and the infographic

Geographic coordinates use EPSG:4326, keeping the Canary Islands in their actual location. EGIF coordinates are transformed only when their coordinate system can be interpreted. Missing coordinates or an unknown datum leave the geographic coordinates empty rather than producing an invented point.

The fire-level view uses interpretable EGIF coordinates where available and an identified municipal reference location otherwise. location_method distinguishes these sources. For fires with several reports, the view records which report supplies its reference point. Declared municipality codes and municipalities obtained through a spatial join are retained separately.

The points are reference locations, not fire perimeters. Municipal reference locations come from IGN through SIANE and mapSpain. The infographic reads the reconciled fire view and uses circle sizes to show forest area burned.

Downloads, citation and reuse

Both products are available in CSV, JSON and GeoJSON from the project website. Read identifiers and municipality codes as text to preserve their representation. JSON supplies explicit types and null values; GeoJSON retains records without usable coordinates with geometry: null.

Machine-readable field descriptions are provided separately in the EGIF report Croissant metadata and the fire-level Croissant metadata.

For reproducible analyses, cite the DOI of the version used. The collection’s version 2.0.0 DOI identifies the archived release; the general DOI groups the project’s releases.

Data reuse follows the MITECO legal notice, including attribution and preservation of the original conditions and metadata. The municipal cartography credits CartoBase ANE 2006–2024, CC BY 4.0, IGN. The repository’s MIT license applies to code and documentation. The project is independent and does not imply MITECO participation or endorsement.

References

  • Royé, D. (2021, June 1). Firefly cartography. Dr Dominic Royé. https://dominicroye.github.io/blog/firefly-maps/

item.title: Let’s peel the world
item.description: Do you know the interrupted Goode homolosine projection?
item.content:encoded:
Do you know the interrupted Goode homolosine projection?

What would happen if we peeled the Earth like an orange? The interrupted Goode homolosine projection gives us something close to that! This equal-area projection preserves relative areas while splitting the world map into lobes. Add a few shades of orange and our world is ready to peel.

Let’s make it with sf, giscoR and ggplot2. First, we get the coastlines and draw the outline, following the cuts between the lobes.

library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(giscoR)
library(showtext)

world <- gisco_get_coastal_lines(resolution = 10)
goode_crs <- "+proj=igh"
lat <- c(90:-90, rep(c(-90:0, 0:-90), 3), -90:90, 90:0, 0:90, 90)
lon <- c(
  rep(180, 181),
  rep(c(80.01, 79.99, -19.99, -20.01, -99.99, -100.01), each = 91),
  rep(-180, 181),
  rep(c(-40.01, -39.99), each = 91),
  180
)
outline <- st_sfc(st_polygon(list(cbind(lon, lat))), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(goode_crs)
rectangle <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(outline) * 1.1)
mask <- st_difference(rectangle, outline)

Next, we draw the meridians and parallels within each lobe so that they do not connect across the cuts.

lobes <- list(
  c(-180, -40, 0, 90), c(-40, 180, 0, 90),
  c(-180, -100, -90, 0), c(-100, -20, -90, 0),
  c(-20, 80, -90, 0), c(80, 180, -90, 0)
)
lines <- lapply(lobes, function(b) {
  west <- b[1] + 0.01
  east <- b[2] - 0.01
  south <- max(b[3], -89.99)
  north <- min(b[4], 89.99)
  meridians <- seq(-180, 180, 30)
  meridians <- meridians[meridians > west & meridians < east]
  parallels <- seq(-60, 60, 30)
  parallels <- parallels[parallels >= south & parallels <= north]
  c(
    lapply(meridians, function(x) {
      st_linestring(cbind(x, seq(south, north, length.out = 181)))
    }),
    lapply(parallels, function(y) {
      st_linestring(cbind(seq(west, east, length.out = 361), y))
    })
  )
})
grat <- st_sfc(do.call(c, lines), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(goode_crs)

Finally, we add the orange palette. The mask hides anything outside the outline and keeps the edges of our peel tidy.

font_add_google("Coiny", family = "coiny")

showtext_auto()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = outline, fill = "#FFF0D9", colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = world, fill = "#F9B566", colour = "#B34D08", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = grat, fill = NA, colour = "#E8A45B", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = mask, fill = "#fcf1e7", colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = outline, fill = NA, colour = "#E87516", linewidth = 0.4) +
  coord_sf(
    crs = goode_crs,
    xlim = st_bbox(outline)[c("xmin", "xmax")],
    ylim = st_bbox(outline)[c("ymin", "ymax")],
    expand = FALSE,
    datum = NA
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = "coiny"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#fcf1e7", colour = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(
      color = "#E87516", face = "bold", size = rel(3),
      margin = margin(b = 10)
    ),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      color = "#E87516", size = rel(1.5),
      margin = margin(t = 10)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Let's peel the world",
    caption = "Interrupted Goode homolosine projection"
  )

References

  • Panaïotis, T. (2026, September 29). Projections cartographiques : Le guide pour ne pas y laisser sa santé mentale. Pyranhia. Article
  • Wilke, C. O. (n.d.). Interrupted Goode homolosine. practicalgg. https://wilkelab.org/practicalgg/articles/goode.html (Source for the outline and masking approach.)

item.title: Conversations across the web with Webmentions
item.description: Bringing mentions, likes and reposts back to the blog
item.content:encoded:
Bringing mentions, likes and reposts back to the blog

Conversations about a blog post often happen somewhere else. Someone shares a link, replies on their own site or reacts to a post on social media. I wanted to bring some of that activity back here.

This implementation was directly inspired by Matt Hobbs’s article, Implementing Webmentions on this blog, published on Nooshu.

I liked its simple presentation: links to mentions and replies, followed by small groups of avatars for likes and reposts. So I added a similar section to this blog, using the typography, colors and buttons from Chulapa.

How it works

A Webmention is a notification that one page links to another. If you write about one of my posts on your own site, you can send its URL so the link can appear below the original article.

This blog already advertised a Webmention.io endpoint. The missing piece was displaying the mentions it had collected. A small JavaScript file now requests the public mentions for each post’s canonical URL and builds the section automatically when the page opens.

Mentions and replies appear as a numbered list of links and authors. Likes and reposts have their own counts and rows of overlapping avatars. The content stays on its original site. Each link takes you to the conversation. The existing GitHub comments are still available, too.

A small addition to a static blog

The implementation uses a Jekyll include, a stylesheet and plain JavaScript. There is no extra Jekyll plugin or change to the deployment workflow. Webmention.io handles receiving and verifying links, while the browser loads the results through its public API.

I tried it with the geobounds post, which already had mentions, and with a recent post that had none. Both cases matter: an empty section should still explain how to join in.

Sharing a link on a social network only brings reactions here if a bridge sends them as Webmentions.

Send a link

Written something that links to this post? Open Shared your thoughts on this post? Drop your link here! below and submit your page’s URL. The form works without JavaScript, although displaying existing mentions requires it.

Thanks to Matt Hobbs for the inspiration and for sharing his implementation. It is a nice way to let a static blog take part in a wider conversation.

AI assistance: I wrote this post with help from Codex, including drafting and editing the text. Codex also helped implement and test the Webmentions section. The header image was also generated with AI.

item.title: Building a documentation chatbot for Chulapa
item.description: A development diary: context, small screens and useful answers
item.content:encoded:
A development diary: context, small screens and useful answers

This website uses my Jekyll theme, Chulapa. Some time ago, I started wondering whether I could add a chatbot to its documentation. The docs already explain the settings, layouts and snippets, but you sometimes need to know what a feature is called before finding it. Could I make that a little easier?

The idea was simple: ask a question, get a useful example and follow a link to the original docs. With Codex, OpenAI’s coding agent, I had an initial version working on the page in less than an hour: I could open the widget, send a question and read its answer. That was the prototype, though. Checking its answers and making it behave properly on a phone took quite a few more rounds.

Start with a prototype, then decide where it belongs

I started with references rather than an empty editor. The freeCodeCamp tutorial on an embeddable chatbot provided a practical starting point for a browser widget backed by Cloudflare Workers. I also liked the visual approach in Malte Grosser’s chatbot post.

I built the implementation with Codex. I described what I wanted, supplied those references and asked it to inspect the existing theme and documentation. There were three pieces to work on: the widget visitors use in the browser, the Worker that processes requests on Cloudflare and a context file containing a summary of the documentation supplied to the model. We worked through them together. I tested the page, asked the chatbot questions and brought back screenshots when something looked wrong. Codex helped turn that feedback into code changes.

Working this way let me spend more time trying the assistant as a visitor would: does this answer help me configure my site? Can I read it with the keyboard open? What happens after a long conversation?

At first, I considered adding the chatbot as a theme feature. That quickly felt like too much to ask of someone who just wants a Jekyll site. An AI account, a separate backend and a maintained knowledge summary would become part of their setup.

So I kept it as an extension of the theme’s documentation site. The implementation and evaluation files live under docs/ai-chatbot/ in the theme repository. Someone using the theme does not need to set up a Worker or maintain an AI context. This also gives me room to experiment without making every experiment part of the template.

A static site with a separate AI backend

Jekyll builds the static documentation pages. I chose a separate service to process the chatbot’s questions. A script loads the chat widget, and a Cloudflare Worker serves the widget and handles questions. The Worker sends the question, instructions and a reviewed documentation summary to Workers AI, Cloudflare’s service for running AI models, then returns the answer to the browser.

The model currently configured is Gemma, using the identifier @cf/google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it. The Worker accesses it through an AI binding: a connection configured in Cloudflare that lets the Worker call Workers AI. That connection stays on the server side, so visitors do not receive an API key. Codex helped me build and test the implementation. Gemma is the model that answers visitors’ questions.

There is no automatic document retrieval in this implementation. The context is a Markdown file maintained alongside the code. Adding a documentation URL or the RSS feed URL gives the model a reference to share. The Worker still relies on the maintained context file for page content and new posts.

That was an intentional starting point. I can inspect exactly which facts the assistant receives, and updating it does not require a vector database or a document indexing pipeline. The tradeoff is that I have to keep that summary current.

Making the answers readable was another part of the interface work. They arrive as Markdown, which Marked converts to HTML for lists, code blocks and links. DOMPurify then removes potentially dangerous HTML before the answer is displayed. Visitors can copy code and follow permitted documentation links. Mentions of the theme use its chulapa class, while code and configuration identifiers retain their original formatting.

The first answers exposed the missing context

One of my first questions was: “Can I add video here?” The answer did not really help. I knew the docs explained how to do it, so I asked Codex to check what the assistant was receiving. The summary needed the video snippet and its options, not just a general mention that videos were supported.

Another exchange made the problem particularly obvious. The theme has built-in skins that change the site’s visual appearance. I asked how to change a skin, and the assistant explained chulapa-skin.skin. Then I asked which skins were available. It replied that there were more than 40, but gave no names. That was related to the question, yet it did not help me choose anything.

I added actual skin names and a link to the visual catalog to the context, along with an instruction to give examples when someone asks what is available. In the follow-up tests, the assistant returned skin names and a link to the catalog instead of just repeating the number of choices. That was a useful improvement I could check directly, even though other answers still needed work. For configuration questions, a small complete example is often more useful than another paragraph. For example, this goes in the site’s _config.yml to select the darkly skin:

chulapa-skin:
  skin: darkly

I expanded the summary selectively: installation, configuration, layouts, videos, galleries, navigation, search, comments, SEO and the FAQ. Later passes added Sass variables and Markdown guidance. I tried to include the details that let someone act: exact option names, defaults, a short example and the right source page.

Copying all the docs into the prompt would have been easier to automate. It would also make each request larger and leave plenty of irrelevant information competing with the answer. The goal was informative help with a manageable context, rather than the longest possible context.

Testing questions instead of counting successful requests

I asked Codex to work through the documentation in batches and send basic and advanced questions to the live assistant. Installation and skin changes were only the beginning. We also checked project-site URLs, favicons, local videos, galleries, highlighting and combinations of settings. I reviewed the results and used the weak answers to decide where the context needed more detail.

I also asked Codex to look for real user questions in the Issues and Discussions of the Chulapa repository. These helped us test the assistant with the wording people actually use when they get stuck, rather than only questions based on documentation headings. We used those questions to prepare evaluation cases and checked the answers against the docs. Feature requests needed particular care: someone asking for an option does not mean the theme already supports it.

We added an evaluation script that sends questions to the live assistant in batches and saves the full responses. That gives me a record to review for the explanation, code and source links. A successful HTTP response only means that the request worked. It says nothing about whether the YAML is correct, the answer covers every part of the question or the link points to the right page.

Some failures were subtle: a plausible option in the wrong place, an incomplete example or a source link with an invented anchor. Follow-up tests helped target those weaknesses. I also included unsupported features and unrelated questions to check whether the assistant would acknowledge missing information.

This process is sometimes called “training the chatbot,” but I did not train or fine-tune the model. I improved the supplied context and instructions, then tested the resulting answers. Those changes can help, but they do not guarantee that every future response will be correct.

A chat history that does not become model memory

The widget keeps recent messages in the tab’s session storage, making it easier to return to an answer while browsing. Each request to the model is independent, however: earlier messages are not sent with the next question. This started as a limitation of the prototype, rather than a deliberate choice to rule out conversational memory, and remains a limitation of the version described here. Keeping the history visible does not change what the backend sends to the model.

That distinction needed to be visible. A familiar chat interface naturally invites questions such as “And what about that one?” Here, it is better to ask a complete question. I added that guidance near the input and a clear-chat control for the local history.

The phone found problems the desktop missed

The interface took several rounds of testing on a real phone. Opening the keyboard could zoom the page or leave the panel clipped. Rotating the phone made the available space even smaller. A desktop browser resized to a narrow width was useful, but it did not reproduce all of those behaviors.

The input now uses a mobile-friendly text size, and the panel follows the space actually visible on screen when the keyboard opens. That available area is called the visual viewport. Using it helps the panel fit above the keyboard. Opening the chat on mobile does not automatically focus the input and summon the keyboard.

Long conversations revealed another bug: a second scrollbar appeared on the outer panel, followed by a large empty area below the form. Constraining the message log and clipping its paint overflow kept scrolling inside the history, with the header and question form visible.

The button that opens the chatbot also had to coexist with the theme’s floating menu button and its separate table-of-contents control. After trying different positions, I settled on stacking the chatbot button above the menu button on smaller screens, matching its size and right margin, with a gap between them. Small alignment differences were much more noticeable than I expected.

I wanted the launcher to fit the site visually and still be easy to recognize. We tried a robot icon first, then settled on a small sparkle SVG for opening the assistant and a paper-plane icon for sending a question. The SVG uses currentColor, so its color follows the button’s CSS instead of being fixed inside the image. That makes it easier to keep the icon consistent with the rest of the control.

Limits and maintenance are part of the implementation

I wanted to keep the experiment within the Free account’s allowance, including the requests we sent while testing. The Worker has input checks, a bounded response length and a rate-limit binding configured for five requests per IP per minute. Live testing eventually produced a rejection, but it also showed that the cutoff was not exactly the sixth request. Cloudflare describes this limiter as approximate and local to each location, meaning a Cloudflare data center, in its Rate Limiting API documentation. It is useful protection, not an exact global usage counter.

The per-IP limit controls how often a visitor can send questions. The account’s quota limits total AI usage. I kept the account on the Free plan without configuring a paid alternative to continue answering when its allowance runs out. The current allowances are listed in Cloudflare’s Workers AI pricing.

To maintain this implementation, I run these commands from the Chulapa repository:

cd docs/ai-chatbot
npm ci
npm run build
npm test
npx wrangler deploy

These commands build, test and deploy the existing Worker. A new chatbot needs additional setup. A GitHub Pages deployment publishes the documentation, while wrangler deploy updates the assistant. Changes to the context reach the live model only after rebuilding and deploying the Worker.

I also added an AGENTS.md file with repository instructions for Codex and other coding agents: when documentation changes, review the assistant’s context and relevant evaluation cases. That makes this check part of the work on the docs, instead of something I have to remember afterward.

What I want this assistant to do well

I want someone to ask a practical question, receive an informative answer and leave with a working example or a useful documentation link. There are still limitations: independent questions require enough detail, combined questions can lose a part of the answer, and source links need continued checking.

You can try it on the Chulapa documentation site. Open the sparkle button and ask a complete question about your setup. I would love to hear which answers helped and which ones sent you back to the docs!

The most useful part of the process was trying the assistant with questions I already knew how to answer. It made the gaps easy to spot: an answer could sound reasonable and still leave me without the setting or example I needed. That is what I want to keep checking as the documentation grows.

AI assistance: I wrote this post with help from Codex, including drafting and editing the text. I reviewed it against the implementation and my experience building the chatbot. The header illustration was also generated with AI.

item.title: Introducing geobounds
item.description: Easy access to administrative boundaries from geoBoundaries
item.content:encoded:
Easy access to administrative boundaries from geoBoundaries

If you’ve ever worked with spatial data in R, this may ring a bell…

  • Search for boundary data
  • Figure out which version is “official”
  • Download a shapefile
  • Unzip it
  • Load it
  • Fix projections
  • Repeat

While searching for new data sources, I found the excellent geoBoundaries database. However, accessing the data can be tedious since it’s provided as zipped shapefiles, and as any GIS professional knows, shapefiles should die!

Previously, the rgeoboundaries package was on CRAN and allowed access to the geoBoundaries API, but it was archived. So I decided to create my own version, and geobounds was born.

  • Source code: https://github.com/dieghernan/geobounds
  • pkgdown website: https://dieghernan.github.io/geobounds/

It connects directly to the excellent geoBoundaries database and returns clean, ready-to-use sf objects with a single function call. No manual downloads and no shapefile handling.

This is how it works.

Installation

geobounds was recently accepted on CRAN, so just install it with:

install.packages("geobounds")

Load the package and other complementary packages:

library(geobounds)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

Getting administrative levels (ADM)

Administrative level 0 (ADM0) corresponds to countries:

# Panama

gb_get_adm0(country = "Panama") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(fill = "#072357") +
  labs(caption = "Source: www.geoboundaries.org")

You can also retrieve multiple administrative levels at once. For example:

# Simplified files
gb_get(country = "Panama", adm_lvl = "all", simplified = TRUE) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = shapeType), color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(vars(shapeType)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(
    title = "Administrative levels of Panama",
    fill = "level",
    caption = "Source: www.geoboundaries.org"
  )

Global Composite Boundaries (CGAZ)

When you download individual country files, each country reflects its own view of borders. This results in:

  • Overlapping boundaries
  • Geographic gaps
  • Disputed territories

For clean global visualizations, geoBoundaries provides a Composite Global Administrative Zones (CGAZ) dataset that can be accessed with gb_get_world().

Here’s an example with country-level files:

# Using individual (gb_get_adm) shapefiles
gb_get_adm0(country = c("India", "Pakistan")) |>
  # Disputed area: Kashmir
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = shapeName), alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#FF671F", "#00401A")) +
  labs(
    fill = "Country",
    title = "Map of India & Pakistan",
    subtitle = "Note the overlap in the Kashmir region",
    caption = "Source: www.geoboundaries.org"
  )

And here’s the same comparison using CGAZ with gb_get_world():

gb_get_world(c("India", "Pakistan")) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = shapeName), alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#FF671F", "#00401A")) +
  labs(
    fill = "Country",
    title = "Map of India & Pakistan",
    subtitle = "CGAZ does not overlap",
    caption = "Source: www.geoboundaries.org"
  )

Understanding the data

The geoBoundaries database undergoes rigorous quality assurance, including manual review and hand-digitization of physical maps. This ensures the highest level of spatial accuracy for scientific and academic research.

This precision comes at a cost: some files can be large and take longer to download. For visualization and general mapping, we recommend using simplified datasets by setting simplified = TRUE.

# Different resolutions
norway <- gb_get_adm0("NOR") |>
  mutate(res = "Full resolution")
print(object.size(norway), units = "Mb")
#> 26.5 Mb

norway_simp <- gb_get_adm0(country = "NOR", simplified = TRUE) |>
  mutate(res = "Simplified")
print(object.size(norway_simp), units = "Mb")
#> 1.5 Mb

norway_all <- bind_rows(norway, norway_simp)

# Plot with ggplot2
ggplot(norway_all) +
  geom_sf(fill = "#BA0C2F", color = "#00205B") +
  facet_wrap(vars(res)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(caption = "Source: www.geoboundaries.org")

Caching

Downloaded files are cached locally. That means:

  • You download once
  • Re-running your script is fast
  • Your workflow stays reproducible

You can set the cache directory with:

gb_set_cache_dir("a/path/to/a/folder")

When should you use geobounds?

Use geobounds when:

  • You need reliable global administrative boundaries
  • You want reproducible workflows
  • You prefer code over manual downloads
  • You’re building maps, dashboards or spatial analyses

Related packages

geobounds is not alone in this space. Depending on your needs, you might also want to look at:

rnaturalearth

A very popular package to access Natural Earth datasets directly from R. It’s lightweight and great for quick global maps, especially at small scales.

If you need physical layers (rivers, coastlines, elevation) alongside political boundaries, this is often a good choice.

giscoR

If your focus is Europe, giscoR provides direct access to Eurostat GISCO data. It’s particularly useful for NUTS regions and European statistical boundaries.

osmdata

When administrative boundaries are not enough and you need OpenStreetMap features (roads, POIs, land use, etc.), osmdata gives you powerful querying capabilities.

Bottom line

I built geobounds to provide direct access to geoBoundaries products. I hope this package will help you in your GIS journey.

Happy mapping!

item.title: Mapping Antarctica
item.description: Cool maps from the South Pole
item.content:encoded:
Cool maps from the South Pole

Creating maps with R is usually straightforward, but representations that cross the International Date Line or that use polar projections can be tricky.

Different spatial-data providers use different conventions: some break geometries at certain longitudes (for example, cutting the Chukchi Peninsula), while others omit portions of the data. These inconsistencies can produce awkward artifacts near the poles.

In this post I fix the GISCO (European Commission) shapefile for Antarctica and produce clean orthographic maps. I walk through the manual corrections and then create a few example maps.

# Libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(giscoR)
library(ggrepel)
library(rmapshaper)

Fixing the geometry

First, we obtain the GISCO Antarctica polygon and transform it to an orthographic projection centered on the South Pole.

antarct <- gisco_get_countries(year = 2024, resolution = 1, country = "ATA") %>%
  select(NAME = NAME_ENGL) |>
  # Orthographic projection centered on the South Pole
  st_transform(crs = "+proj=ortho +lat_0=-90 +lon_0=0")

ggplot(antarct) +
  geom_sf(fill = "lightblue")

The shapefile contains a visible “lollipop” cut that looks unnatural in an orthographic projection. I correct it manually with these steps:

  1. Identify the polygon that represents the main Antarctic landmass.
  2. Convert that polygon to a sequence of coordinates (points).
  3. Remove the small sequence of points that create the artifact.
  4. Rebuild the polygon from the cleaned coordinates and replace the broken geometry with the corrected one.

We convert polygons to point coordinates and inspect them to find the offending sequence:

# Identify the largest polygon
ant_explode <- antarct |>
  st_cast("POLYGON")

nrow(ant_explode)
#> [1] 778

# Largest polygon

ant_max <- ant_explode[which.max(st_area(ant_explode)), ]

coords <- st_coordinates(ant_max) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  # Add an ID for the points
  mutate(np = row_number())


ggplot(coords, aes(X, Y)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.05, color = "darkblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = np), check_overlap = TRUE) +
  coord_equal()

From the plotted indices, we can see the problematic points fall roughly in the range 8200–9200. We inspect that interval in detail to select the exact indices to remove.

test <- coords |>
  filter(np %in% seq(8200, 9200))

test |>
  ggplot(aes(X, Y)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.05, color = "darkblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = np), check_overlap = TRUE)

Note: This cleaning is tailored to this specific shapefile and may need to be repeated for other shapefiles. The approach is straightforward but depends on the particular geometry and projection. 
# Final solution after some iterations...

test |>
  filter(np %in% seq(8289, 9130)) |>
  ggplot(aes(X, Y)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = "To remove")


test |>
  filter(!np %in% seq(8289, 9130)) |>
  ggplot(aes(X, Y)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkblue") +
  labs(title = "To keep")
After removing the offending points, we rebuild the polygon and reconstitute the full Antarctica shape from the corrected piece plus the remaining polygons. 
# From coordinates to polygon
newpol <- coords |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  filter(!np %in% seq(8289, 9130)) |> # Removing offending points
  select(X, Y) |>
  as.matrix() |>
  list() |>
  st_polygon() |>
  st_sfc() |>
  st_set_crs(st_crs(ant_max))

ant_max_fixed <- st_sf(st_drop_geometry(ant_max), geometry = newpol)

# Regenerate initial shape
antarctica_fixed <- bind_rows(
  ant_max_fixed,
  ant_explode[-which.max(st_area(ant_explode)), ]
) |>
  group_by(NAME) |>
  summarise(m = 1) |>
  select(-m) |>
  st_make_valid()

antarctica_fixed
#> Simple feature collection with 1 feature and 1 field
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -2583099 ymin: -2458296 xmax: 2690846 ymax: 2233395
#> Projected CRS: +proj=ortho +lat_0=-90 +lon_0=0
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   NAME                                                                     geometry
#> * <chr>                                                          <MULTIPOLYGON [m]>
#> 1 Antarctica (((-2456385 1179033, -2456141 1178965, -2456464 1178341, -2456563 117…

ggplot(antarctica_fixed) +
  geom_sf(fill = "lightblue")

Plotting examples

With the corrected shape we can produce maps. Below are a few examples based on proposed Antarctic flag designs.

Graham Bartram’s proposal (1996)

A simple rendition of Bartram’s original concept:

bbox <- st_bbox(antarctica_fixed) # For limits on the panel

antarctica_fixed |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(fill = "white", color = NA) +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#009fdc"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(title = "Graham Bartram's proposal") +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = c(bbox[c(1, 3)]) * 1.8,
    ylim = c(bbox[c(2, 4)]) * 1.4
  )

Emblem of the Antarctic Treaty

This example uses graticules to create a concentric “bullseye” pattern around Antarctica. Generating such graticules and merging meridians requires a few extra steps to avoid small gaps near the pole.

# Need graticules
grats <- giscoR::gisco_get_countries() |>
  st_transform(st_crs(antarctica_fixed)) |>
  # Specify the cuts of the graticules
  st_graticule(
    lat = c(-80, -70, -60),
    lon = seq(-180, 180, 30),
    ndiscr = 10000,
    margin = 0.000001
  )


ggplot(grats) +
  geom_sf(color = "darkblue")

We merge meridians so the area around the South Pole is filled. st_graticule() can leave a tiny hole at the pole, and we fix this by joining complementary meridians.

# Merge meridians
merid <- lapply(seq(-180, 0, 30), function(x) {
  df <- grats |>
    filter(type == "E") |>
    filter(degree %in% c(x, x + 180))

  df2 <- df |>
    st_geometry() |>
    st_cast("MULTIPOINT") |>
    st_union() |>
    st_cast("LINESTRING")

  sf_x <- st_sf(
    degree = x,
    type = "E",
    geometry = df2
  )
}) |> bind_rows()


grats_end <- merid |>
  bind_rows(grats |>
    filter(type != "E"))

We then cut and color the resulting graticules so they form the emblem-like pattern.

# Cut since some grats should be colored differently

antarctica_simp <- rmapshaper::ms_simplify(antarctica_fixed, keep = 0.005)
grats_yes <- st_intersection(grats_end, antarctica_simp)
grats_no <- st_difference(grats_end, antarctica_simp)

antarctica_simp |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(fill = "white", color = NA) +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#072b5f"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = grats_yes, color = "#072b5f", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_sf(data = grats_no, color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = c(bbox[c(1, 3)]) * 1.8,
    ylim = c(bbox[c(2, 4)]) * 1.4
  ) +
  labs(title = "Emblem of the Antarctic Treaty")

Antarctica flag redesigned

In 2024, Graham Bartram revealed a new version of his original flag as part of a global campaign to raise awareness about the growing problem of microplastic pollution. The new design keeps the familiar white outline of Antarctica but swaps the plain blue background for one filled with countless tiny, colorful dots. These dots represent the microscopic bits of plastic that have been discovered even in the planet’s most untouched places, including the Antarctic ice and its surrounding oceans.

Because the design relies on randomness, we approximate it using the following procedure:

  1. Sample random points across the Antarctic polygon.
  2. Build Voronoi polygons from those points, then apply a small negative buffer to create gaps.
  3. Randomly sample the resulting polygons to increase visual noise.
  4. Color polygons so larger areas remain white while smaller polygons use magenta/pink tones.
# Maximum chunk of Antarctica, the one that we fixed

ant_max_fixed
#> Simple feature collection with 1 feature and 1 field
#> Geometry type: POLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -2447764 ymin: -2125910 xmax: 2690846 ymax: 2233395
#> Projected CRS: +proj=ortho +lat_0=-90 +lon_0=0
#>         NAME                       geometry
#> 1 Antarctica POLYGON ((-2423737 1557908,...

set.seed(2024)
# Sample, Voronoi and negative buffer
plastics <- st_sample(ant_max_fixed, 3000) |>
  st_union() |>
  st_voronoi(envelope = st_geometry(ant_max_fixed)) |>
  st_collection_extract() |>
  st_buffer(dist = -10000)


# Keep only those properly included in the outline

toinc <- st_contains_properly(ant_max_fixed, plastics, sparse = FALSE) |>
  as.vector()

# Select random chunks
plastic_end <- plastics[toinc, ] |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  slice_sample(prop = 0.75)

ggplot(plastic_end) +
  geom_sf(fill = "darkblue")




# Random coloring

plastic_end$area <- st_area(plastic_end) |> as.double()

plastic_end$fill <- sample(c("#ff00ec", "#9e00ec"), nrow(plastic_end), replace = TRUE)
plastic_end$fill <- ifelse(plastic_end$area > quantile(plastic_end$area, probs = 0.4),
  "white",
  plastic_end$fill
)

bbox2 <- st_bbox(plastic_end)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = plastic_end, aes(fill = fill), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#009fdc"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(title = "New redesign") +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = c(bbox2[c(1, 3)] * 1.8),
    ylim = c(bbox2[c(2, 4)]) * 1.4
  )

item.title: Implementing group_by count in Liquid
item.content:encoded:
See the magic happening

Liquid is a template language used by Jekyll, the static site generator behind this website and my theme, Chulapa (link).

Some time ago, @cargocultprogramming reported a broken theme component in dieghernan/chulapa#29. The problem appeared with Jekyll 4.1.0 and was also reported in jekyll/jekyll#8214.

The affected code used group_by to count repeated strings in an array:


{% assign alldocs = site.exercises %}
{% assign grouptag = alldocs | map: 'tags' | join: ',' | split: ',' | group_by: tag %}
{{ grouptag }}

In that example, tag is an undefined variable, rather than the name of a property on each item. Jekyll 4.0.1 produced separate groups for the strings, but 4.1.0 placed them in a single group with an empty name. This specific usage changed. Grouping objects by a named property remains supported.

The workaround below counts string occurrences without custom plugins. It uses Liquid templates with Jekyll-specific filters, including where_exp and push, so it is not portable to every Liquid environment. where_exp requires Jekyll 3.2.0 or later. The live examples run with the version used to build this site.

The algorithm is implemented in Chulapa. The expandable tables use this site’s documents and change as posts are added. You can also see the tags on the /tags page.

Counting tag occurrences

For a small example, an input array of ['ruby', 'jekyll', 'ruby'] gives these two parallel arrays:

single_tags = ['ruby', 'jekyll']
count_tags  = [2, 1]

There are two distinct tags. Each position in count_tags holds the number of occurrences of the tag at the same position in single_tags.

First, collect the tags from site.documents. Then keep the unique tags and count how often each appears in the full array:


{% assign alldocs = site.documents %}
{% assign alltags = alldocs | map: 'tags' | join: ',' | split: ',' %}
{% assign single_tags = alltags | uniq %}
{% assign count_tags = '' | split: ',' %}

{% for tag in single_tags %}
  {% assign count_this_tag = alltags | where_exp: "item", "item == tag" | size %}
  {% assign count_tags = count_tags | push: count_this_tag %}
{% endfor %}

The join and split filters flatten the tag arrays using a comma as a separator. This assumes that tag names contain no commas. The algorithm counts occurrences, so a repeated tag within one document would be counted more than once. Tag comparisons are case-sensitive.

To display the counts, iterate over the unique tags and use forloop.index0 to retrieve the corresponding count. An empty input produces no table rows.


<table>
  <caption>Tag counts on this site</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Tag</th>
      <th scope="col">Count</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    {% for tag in single_tags %}
      <tr>
        <td>{{ tag | escape }}</td>
        <td>{{ count_tags[forloop.index0] }}</td>
      </tr>
    {% endfor %}
  </tbody>
</table>

Sorting

To sort by descending frequency, find the largest count and work down to one. For each frequency, append the matching tags and their counts to two new arrays. This approach is also used in Minimal Mistakes.


{% assign sorted_tags = '' | split: ',' %}
{% assign sorted_count_tags = '' | split: ',' %}

{% if single_tags.size > 0 %}
  {% assign n_tags = single_tags | size | minus: 1 %}
  {% assign items_max = count_tags | sort | last %}
  {% for i in (1..items_max) reversed %}
    {% for j in (0..n_tags) %}
      {% if count_tags[j] == i %}
        {% assign sorted_tags = sorted_tags | push: single_tags[j] %}
        {% assign sorted_count_tags = sorted_count_tags | push: i %}
      {% endif %}
    {% endfor %}
  {% endfor %}
{% endif %}

Tags with equal counts retain their order of first appearance in alltags. The empty-input check avoids constructing index ranges or finding a maximum when there are no tags. Each unique tag is appended once, so a final uniq filter is unnecessary.


<table>
  <caption>Tag counts in descending order</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th scope="col">Tag</th>
      <th scope="col">Count</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    {% for tag in sorted_tags %}
      <tr>
        <td>{{ tag | escape }}</td>
        <td>{{ sorted_count_tags[forloop.index0] }}</td>
      </tr>
    {% endfor %}
  </tbody>
</table>

The counting step scans all tag occurrences for each unique tag, requiring roughly O(U * N) comparisons, where U is the number of unique tags and N is the total number of occurrences. The nested sorting loops perform O(U * M) comparisons, where M is the largest count. Array copying by push adds overhead. This is practical for small blogs, but large sites may benefit from computing tag counts outside the template.

Complete example

Here is the combined counting and sorting code. The resulting sorted_tags and sorted_count_tags arrays can be displayed with the table above.


{% assign alldocs = site.documents %}
{% assign alltags = alldocs | map: 'tags' | join: ',' | split: ',' %}
{% assign single_tags = alltags | uniq %}
{% assign count_tags = '' | split: ',' %}

{% for tag in single_tags %}
  {% assign count_this_tag = alltags | where_exp: "item", "item == tag" | size %}
  {% assign count_tags = count_tags | push: count_this_tag %}
{% endfor %}

{% assign sorted_tags = '' | split: ',' %}
{% assign sorted_count_tags = '' | split: ',' %}

{% if single_tags.size > 0 %}
  {% assign n_tags = single_tags | size | minus: 1 %}
  {% assign items_max = count_tags | sort | last %}
  {% for i in (1..items_max) reversed %}
    {% for j in (0..n_tags) %}
      {% if count_tags[j] == i %}
        {% assign sorted_tags = sorted_tags | push: single_tags[j] %}
        {% assign sorted_count_tags = sorted_count_tags | push: i %}
      {% endif %}
    {% endfor %}
  {% endfor %}
{% endif %}

item.title: Happy Valentine’s Day
item.description: Do you know the Bonne projection?
item.content:encoded:
Do you know the Bonne projection?

Do you know the Bonne Projection? This is a very special one, as it produces this result when used to map the whole world. Happy Valentine’s Day!

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(giscoR)
library(ggplot2)
library(showtext)


world <- gisco_get_countries()

# Shaped ocean

h_earth <- world %>%
  # Fine grid
  st_make_grid(n = c(50, 50)) %>%
  # Bonne projection
  st_transform("ESRI:54024") %>%
  # To sf object (data-frame like)
  st_sf(couple = 2, someval = 1, .)


# And finally

font_add_google(name = "Emilys Candy", family = "emilys")

showtext_auto()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = h_earth, fill = "#f9b7bb", color = "#f9b7bb") +
  geom_sf(data = world, fill = "#d24658", color = "#d24658") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Happy Valentine's Day",
    caption = "Bonne Projection (ESRI:54024)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#faddcf",
      color = "transparent"
    ),
    text = element_text(family = "emilys", colour = "#d24658"),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = rel(3)),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = rel(2))
  )
